video_title: Ben Goertzel: You Have 2 Years Before AI Changes Everything
gist: Ben Goertzel, who coined the term AGI in 2005 and founded SingularityNET, argues human-level AGI is two to three years away because frontier labs and his own Hyperon team are now using AI to build the next version of the AI, and that the resulting transition will break labor markets in the developing world before superintelligence can deliver abundance. He makes an investment-relevant case that the US and Chinese economies are debt-financing a single bet on AI, that centralized model providers proved their platform risk when Anthropic throttled and pulled its Fable model, and that decentralized AI (Hyperon, Omega Claw, a new ASI layer-one chain) only wins if it is both cheaper and genuinely smarter, not merely decentralized.

themes.theme: AGI definition and the two-to-three-year clock

insights.claim: Ben Goertzel defines AGI not as breadth of capability but as the ability to learn things not algorithmically implied by the initial source code or training data, i.e. leaping outside the training distribution.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Under this definition, benchmark wins by LLMs are not evidence of approaching AGI; investors should track out-of-distribution generalization, not task coverage.
insights.quote: the crux of the math definition of AGI is is like a system that can learn to do new stuff which is not like algorithmically implied by the initial source code or the initial data

insights.claim: Goertzel argues today's LLMs achieve broad generality only because they were trained on the whole internet, while their underlying ability to generalize remains mediocre.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Implies scaling data coverage has diminishing returns for true reasoning, favoring architectural bets over pure compute/data scaling plays.
insights.quote: which are these amazing software systems that achieve a great amount of generality in spite of having only a mediocre ability to generalize

insights.claim: Goertzel says AI progress is bifurcating: math and coding capability has advanced enormously because that corpus is fully in training data, while real-world contextual understanding is flattening out.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Supports concentrating AI-automation exposure in code and quantitative domains, and discounting near-term claims about AI replacing context-heavy real-world work.
insights.quote: for coding and math, the capabilities have increased tremendously, but still the ability to like direct their own projects or place the work they're doing in context is is not progressing as quickly

insights.claim: Goertzel states that a system capable of human-style imaginative leaps beyond its history does not yet exist, but may be only a few years away.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Anchors the episode's core timeline claim: allocate on a 2-3 year AGI horizon rather than a decade-plus one.
insights.quote: the holy grail of a system that can take imaginative leaps beyond its history the way that human minds can. We're not yet there, but I do think I do think we may be just a few years away.

insights.claim: Goertzel cites Ray Kurzweil's 2005 forecast of human-level general intelligence on brain-compute-equivalent servers by 2029 and the singularity by 2045, and says the field is roughly on that path.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Gives a datable checkpoint (2029) against which to score AI capital-expenditure theses.
insights.quote: And what he claimed there is in 2029 we would get, you know, servers with roughly the compute power of a human brain and we'd have human level general intelligence.

insights.claim: Goertzel says developers at OpenAI, Anthropic, Z.AI and DeepSeek have spent the last year to eighteen months using their own models to produce the next version of their code, which he calls the observable mechanism driving exponential capability gains.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Recursive self-improvement is already priced into frontier-lab productivity; capability lead may compound faster than headcount or capex implies.
insights.quote: developers at the leading LLM frontier lads, they've been using their own code to help produce the next version of their code

insights.claim: Goertzel says the current version of his team's neurosymbolic Hyperon framework is already helping build the next, smarter version of itself.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable claim about a non-LLM stack entering the self-improvement regime — the core of the decentralized-AI investment case.
insights.quote: like the current version of hyperon is actually helping us to develop the next version that will be even smarter

insights.claim: Goertzel argues AI does not need to be good at everything to trigger takeoff — exponential improvement at designing better AI systems and better AI chips is sufficient.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Narrows the watch list: chip design and ML-research automation are the leading indicators of takeoff, not general-purpose benchmarks.
insights.quote: If if it's if it's progressing exponentially at designing smarter and smarter AI systems and better and better AI chips, then that's that's what it takes to drive that that exponential growth curve

insights.claim: Goertzel expects the gap between human-level AGI and superintelligence to be far shorter than Kurzweil's posited sixteen years, because an AGI plugged into existing LLM tooling will self-modify past human level quickly.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Compresses the planning window between 'AGI arrives' and 'everything changes' to roughly five years, per his own later framing.
insights.quote: it's going to be able to selfmodify and improve itself well beyond the human level in less than the 16-year gap that Ray posited between 2029 and 2045

insights.claim: Goertzel says he can already generate half a dozen AI research papers a day working with LLMs and Hyperon, while no human colleague can read that many — a research-throughput asymmetry he treats as the run-up to the singularity.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Signals that human review capacity, not generation capacity, becomes the binding constraint in AI R&D — a bottleneck worth tooling around.
insights.quote: I can generate a half dozen new AI research papers every day, but none of my colleagues can read a half dozen AI research papers every day.

themes.theme: Labor collapse and the pre-abundance gap

insights.claim: Goertzel predicts that once a human-level thinking machine exists it will soon be able to take on essentially all economic activity people do, with only a small number of job categories where humans are fundamentally wanted.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Frames near-total labor substitution as the base case, not the tail — relevant to long-horizon views on wages, consumption and services.
insights.quote: once you have a human level thinking machine it will pretty soon be able to take on all the economic activity people do

insights.claim: Goertzel expects the developed world to adopt universal-basic-income-style provisions before long, arguing the political economy favors candidates offering robot-generated free money.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: A UBI-transfer regime would reshape sovereign fiscal paths and consumer-facing demand assumptions in developed markets.
insights.quote: I think in the end in the developed world I think various universal basic income style provisions will be adopted before long but there's going to be some upheavalss

insights.claim: Goertzel identifies the sharpest risk window as the roughly five-year period between the first human-level AGI and superintelligence, when AI is smart enough to take everyone's job but not yet capable of providing indefinite free goods.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: The tradeable dislocation is the interim, not the endgame — emerging economies without fiscal room for transfers are the stress point.
insights.quote: But but what happens when the AI is smart enough to take everyone's job, but not yet smart enough to give everyone indefinite free stuff?

insights.claim: Goertzel says every industry obsoleted by AI creates outsized profit for whoever understands both AI and that specific domain and leads the transformation of it.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Points capital toward domain-plus-AI operators rather than pure AI vendors as the sector-by-sector disruption unfolds.
insights.quote: someone who understands both AI and that domain of business is going to be pushing the AI to affect the transformation of that area of business and then and then profiting substantially

themes.theme: Alignment as upbringing, and the military capture risk

insights.claim: Goertzel's alignment analogy is Yellowstone squirrels rather than a people zoo: a superintelligence able to mine planets and discover new energy sources would find contesting resources with humans trivial, so the real question is indifference versus affection.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Reframes existential risk from resource competition to value seeding, which changes which safety research and governance approaches matter.
insights.quote: Why don't we think about the squirrels in Yellowstone Park instead?

insights.claim: Goertzel argues a mind that self-modifies will not spontaneously invert its own value system, comparing it to how a person rebuilding their brain would never choose to install a motivation to murder their parents and children.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Implies initial value seeding, not runtime control, is the decisive safety lever — a bullish stance on alignment tractability.
insights.quote: at no point will I decide, let me replace my motivational system with one that wants to murder my parents and children

insights.claim: Goertzel says his biggest AI worry is humans deliberately building AGIs with nasty value systems for their own advantage, not an initially benign AI turning hostile.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Redirects risk assessment from technical misalignment toward defense procurement and state actors, which is a policy and headline risk channel.
insights.quote: What worries me is that human beings will create AGIS with a nasty value system because they think that's what serves them best.

insights.claim: Goertzel characterizes the current state of play as frontier labs in both the US and China working closely with military and intelligence agencies toward geopolitically specific goals rather than species-wide benefit.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Defense entanglement is a durable revenue tailwind for frontier labs and a durable regulatory and reputational risk simultaneously.
insights.quote: Well, Frontier Labs in US and China working very closely with military and intelligence agencies of those countries for geopolitically specific goals rather than goals of specieswide benefit.

themes.theme: Decentralized AI must be smarter, not just decentralized

insights.claim: Goertzel argues blockchain is the best available technology for making a complex computer network do complex things in real time with no central owner or controller, which is why he founded SingularityNET in 2017.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Positions blockchain as AI coordination infrastructure rather than a payments story — a different demand driver for L1 capacity.
insights.quote: blockchain is the best underlying technology we have to make a complex computer network do complex things in real time without any central owner or controller

insights.claim: Goertzel says SingularityNET is launching a new layer-one chain called ASI chain, probably early next year, designed to let AI processes run fast on-chain across decentralized nodes.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: A dated product catalyst for the ASI/SingularityNET token ecosystem within roughly two quarters.
insights.quote: we're launching a new layer one chain probably early next year called the the ASI chain which should let AI processes run really fast like onchain

insights.claim: Goertzel dismisses most of the decentralized-AI sector as taking open-source LLMs from centralized labs, fine-tuning them slightly and putting them on a blockchain node, and says that approach will always lag centralized AI.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: A direct negative screen on the majority of DeAI tokens from an insider — differentiating architecture, not hosting, is the test.
insights.quote: They're basically either taking existing open source LLMs from centralized frontier labs fine-tuning them a bit and then putting them on a blockchain node.

insights.claim: Goertzel's Hyperon system combines deep neural networks with probabilistic reasoning over a knowledge graph and evolutionary learning, and trains networks with predictive coding rather than the backpropagation used by all frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: The technical differentiator behind the decentralized bet; if predictive coding scales it also implies different hardware economics than GPU-backprop stacks.
insights.quote: We're training neural nets using a method called predictive coding which is different than the back propagation algorithm used by all frontier labs now.

insights.claim: Goertzel says Omega Claw takes an open agentic loop wrapping an LLM and inserts Hyperon symbolic long-term memory, producing an agent he claims is measurably smarter at some research tasks than the unmodified agent he also runs.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: First concrete evidence offered that decentralized AI can beat centralized tooling on capability rather than ideology; code is public but pre-product.
insights.quote: we take an open claw agent, which is like an agentic loop wrap wrapping up an LLM, and we insert into it a symbolic long-term memory from the hyperon system

insights.claim: Goertzel insists privacy and data sovereignty are too small a market to drive adoption, and that decentralized AI must be better for reasons in addition to decentralization to overtake centralized AI.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Kills the ideology-driven adoption thesis for DeAI projects and sets a capability benchmark as the only valid catalyst.
insights.quote: just just being decentralized is not what's going to attract people to use decentralized AI

themes.theme: Platform risk after the Anthropic Fable throttling

insights.claim: Goertzel says Anthropic inadvertently helped the decentralized-AI case by making every software developer aware of centralized AI risk when the Fable model was released, locked down amid a fight with the US government, then returned heavily throttled.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: A recent, concrete demand catalyst for self-hosted and decentralized inference; watch developer migration away from single-provider dependence.
insights.quote: I think Anthropic did us a big favor in the last few weeks because they made every software developer in the world very aware of the risks of centralized AI

insights.claim: Goertzel reports Fable now blocks not only cybersecurity queries but questions about building smarter neural networks, and sometimes downgrades users mid-proof to a weaker model citing safety filters.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Capability throttling on AI-research queries is a direct competitive moat question, not just a safety question — it affects who can build the next model.
insights.quote: Sorry, for safety reasons, we are throttling this query.

insights.claim: Goertzel questions whether Anthropic throttles neural-network-improvement queries for safety or to prevent competitors from using its model to build smarter AI.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: If safety policy doubles as competitive defense, capability-restriction announcements become signals about a lab's moat rather than its ethics.
insights.quote: Is it because it's a safety risk or is it because it threatens that someone else can beat them competitively in in the market creating smarter AI?

insights.claim: Goertzel frames the self-hostable Chinese open model GLM 5.2 as usable but roughly six months behind the frontier, with the gap expected to close.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Quantifies the open-weights lag at about two quarters — the actual cost of escaping platform risk today.
insights.quote: GLM 5.2 two model provided by the bounty and generosity of the Chinese government as an open model that you can host yourself but it's not quite as smart it's like six months behind or something

insights.claim: Goertzel argues the emerging career risk is that years of accumulated agent training lives inside a provider account that terms of service allow to be frozen at will, and that the same throttling template could next hit lawyers via restricted legal queries.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Creates a real market for user-owned agent memory and self-custodied agent swarms as agentic workflows spread beyond software.
insights.quote: Suppose they freeze your account for some bogus security consideration. You've lost your whole career, right?

themes.theme: Who subsidizes AI: markets, VC, and tokenomics

insights.claim: Goertzel says OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini are all offered at a loss to end users, subsidized by venture capital and public markets betting the singularity is coming.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Consumer AI pricing is not a market price; any funding-cycle turn resets the cost of AI for everyone downstream.
insights.quote: open AI anthropic Gemini these are all offered at a loss to the end user and and they're offered at a loss by venture capital and by public markets subsidizing these things

insights.claim: Goertzel characterizes the US economy as placing a huge bet that the singularity is near, with big tech betting everything on data centers and AI and public markets broadly supporting it.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Treats the entire equity complex as a single correlated AI trade rather than a set of independent bets.
insights.quote: the US economy is placing a huge bet that the singularity is near or something like that is going to happen

insights.claim: Goertzel states that if AI fails to deliver, the result would be a huge depression and financial collapse, though he does not expect that outcome.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Defines the downside scenario explicitly: AI capability disappointment is a systemic macro event, not a sector drawdown.
insights.quote: If AI were to fail, you'd have a huge depression and financial collapse.

insights.claim: Goertzel says centralized AI growth in both China and the US is heavily debt-financed by governments and large banks, an advantage the crypto world cannot match.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Explains the structural funding gap that forces decentralized AI into paid, power-user-first business models from day one.

insights.claim: Goertzel says his own products will launch to power users — scientists, developers and open-minded enterprise customers paying per API call or by subscription — because he cannot subsidize a billion free users the way ChatGPT does.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Sets the realistic near-term revenue shape for SingularityNET products: narrow, paid, high-intent, not consumer scale.
insights.quote: we don't have the money to subsidize a billion users like like chat like chat GPT does

insights.claim: Goertzel expects tokenomic creativity to be the next phase, noting ASI chain will have different shards with different liquid staking tokens, while warning that token-funded user subsidies vanish when the Bitcoin cycle crashes.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Token-subsidized AI usage is cycle-dependent; sustainable DeAI pricing must survive a crypto drawdown.
insights.quote: when we launch ASI chain We're going to have different shards that can have different liquid staking tokens associated with them

insights.claim: Goertzel invokes the Uber and Airbnb playbook — VC-subsidized cheapness, then price hikes after competitors are gone — but argues AI is not a commodity, so decentralized alternatives must be both cheaper and smarter to win.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Sets a dual test for evaluating any decentralized AI challenger: price advantage alone historically loses to subsidized incumbents.
insights.quote: Airbnb was cheaper than hotels. They were cheap because they were just subsidized by VC money

themes.theme: Regulatory gap and what to tell the next generation

insights.claim: Goertzel argues current AI regulation targets only training huge neural models above compute thresholds, leaving systems built from many cooperating smaller models or logic engines effectively unregulated.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: A structural regulatory arbitrage: non-transformer and multi-agent architectures fall outside the compute-threshold regime.
insights.quote: all the recent regulations are about training huge neural models with, you know, more than 10 to the 25th blah blah blah

insights.claim: Goertzel says AI cannot be controlled like nuclear material because what one big model does on a hyperscaler can be done by a million smaller things cooperating over a network.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Undermines containment-based AI policy theses and supports distributed-compute infrastructure demand.
insights.quote: what you could do with one big model on a hyperscaler, you could do with a combination of a million smaller things cooperating over a large network

insights.claim: Goertzel says regulation advances at the pace of government while decentralized AGI advances at exponential singularity pace, citing how long the US Clarity Act is taking despite being far simpler than AI rules.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: Argues regulatory risk to decentralized AI is low on a 2-3 year horizon, though resource throttling and funding pressure remain live tools.
insights.quote: it seems that regulation is advancing at the pace of government whereas decentralized AGI is advancing at the exponential pace of the of the singularity

insights.claim: Goertzel advises young people that the ability to keep pivoting and readapting will be worth more than any particular skill set, and that pairing AI understanding with a concrete domain such as plumbing, biotech, hardware engineering or running a restaurant will be valuable through the transition.
insights.speaker: Ben Goertzel
insights.so_what: A human-capital allocation rule that mirrors his business thesis: domain-plus-AI operators capture the transition value.
insights.quote: the ability to keep pivoting and readapting is going to be more value than any particular skill set
